text:
Opponents fear massive sales tax increases on low- and middle-class earners; proponents see benefits of more money to spend.��

Amendment 1: State parks, soil and water conservation, and historic sites sales tax
Question: Shall Missouri continue for 10 years the one-tenth of one percent sales/use tax that is used for soil and water conservation and for state parks and historic sites, and resubmit this tax to the voters for approval in 10 years?
If passed, Amendment 1 will not increase or decrease taxes. The measure will allow continued collection of the existing sales and use tax for another 10 years, to fund soil and water conservation, state parks and historic sites. The tax currently generates approximately $140 million of revenue annually. Half of that sum goes to the state parks and historic sites managed by the Department of Natural Resources and the other half goes to soil and water conservation districts across Missouri. This tax has been renewed every 10 years since 1984. It was most recently renewed in 2016 with 80% of the vote.
Amendment 2: Charter county assessor requirements
Question: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: require all charter counties, including Jackson County, to provide for the election of a county assessor; and require assessors in all charter counties to comply with any training requirements established by general law?
If passed, Amendment 2 would require all charter counties to elect a county assessor, responsible for classifying and maintaining a current list of all taxable personal property in a county. Currently, Jackson County is the only charter county that appoints its own assessor instead of holding an election for the position. The amendment would also require assessors to meet training requirements set by state law. Missouri���s five charter counties are St. Louis County, Jackson County, St. Charles County, Jefferson County and Clay County.
Amendment 4: Initiative petition changes
Question: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: Modify current requirements that a statewide majority of voters may approve initiative petitions to amend the constitution; Require a majority of voters in each congressional district to approve initiative petitions to amend the constitution; and Make available to each voter the full text of initiative petitions with their ballot?
If passed, Amendment 4 would make it significantly harder for voters to change the state constitution using the initiative petition process. The initiative petition process allows voters to collect a certain amount of signatures and place a proposed amendment on a ballot for a vote. If voters approve Amendment 4, initiative petitions to change the Missouri Constitution would need support from a majority of voters in each congressional district, instead of a simple statewide majority. Based on voting data from 2024, that would mean approximately 5% of Missouri voters could kill a measure that a majority of voters statewide voted to pass. Amendment 4 would only affect measures placed on the ballot by voters, not measures placed on the ballot by legislators.
Amendment 5: Income tax phase-out and sales taxes increase
Question: Shall the Missouri Constitution be amended to: Require legislative phase-out of the individual state income tax based on revenue growth, and authorize the expansion of sales and use taxes; Curtail constitutional limits on taxing goods and services; and Require local tax rate cuts without reducing school funding if local sales tax revenue increases?
If passed, Amendment 5 would slowly phase out state income taxes and give lawmakers the ability to broadly raise sales taxes. Income taxes currently make up about two-thirds of Missouri's general revenue funds. To make up for that gap, the amendment allows state lawmakers to broadly tax all goods and services in the state. Lawmakers would decide what to tax and at what rate over the next five years.
Under the proposal, the cuts to the income tax must be proportional to increases in revenue from new sales taxes. Because of this, both Democratic and Republican state lawmakers called the measure a "tax shift" rather than a blanket tax cut before the measure passed the state legislature.
